items.question: Assess the achievements of Gautamiputra Satakarni as the greatest ruler of the Satavahana dynasty, with reference to the Nasik Prashasti.
items.modelAnswer: **Gautamiputra Satakarni (c. 106–130 CE)** is regarded as the **greatest and most powerful Satavahana ruler**, credited with **reviving the empire's strength** after a period of Shaka pressure. **Militarily**, he defeated the **Shakas, Pahlavas and Yavanas**, most notably crushing the **Shaka king Nahapana**, and expanded his empire from **Malwa, Saurashtra and Konkan to Vidarbha and the Krishna River** in the south. Our principal source for his reign is the **Nasik Prashasti**, an inscription composed by his mother **Gautami Balashri**, which records his conquests and his **patronage of Brahmanism**; here he is celebrated as **Ekabrahmana ('the unique Brahmin')** and as the restorer of Brahmin pride and the four-fold varna order. Yet his rule also reflects **religious accommodation**: despite championing Brahmanism, he **made land grants to Buddhist monks**, an early example of the Satavahana practice of religious endowments. The Prashasti, written by a queen-mother, also illuminates the **matronymic tradition** and the elevated status of women in Satavahana society. In sum, Gautamiputra combined **military recovery, territorial expansion, Brahmanical revival and religious tolerance**, making him the defining figure of Satavahana greatness.
keyPoints: Greatest Satavahana ruler; revived the empire's power.
Defeated the Shakas, Pahlavas and Yavanas — especially the Shaka king Nahapana.
Nasik Prashasti composed by his mother Gautami Balashri; he is styled Ekabrahmana.
Empire extended from Malwa/Saurashtra/Konkan to Vidarbha and the Krishna River.
Championed Brahmanism yet granted land to Buddhist monks — religious accommodation.
The Prashasti also reflects the matronymic tradition and status of women.

items.question: Discuss the contribution of the Satavahanas to art, architecture and trade, highlighting their relevance to the history of Andhra Pradesh.
items.modelAnswer:
The Satavahanas, the **first great kingdom of the Deccan** with capitals at **Pratishthana (Paithan)** and **Amaravati**, made lasting contributions to **art, architecture and trade** — many of them rooted in what is today **Andhra Pradesh**.

In **art and architecture**, their patronage produced the celebrated **Amaravati Stupa** on the Krishna, begun in the 3rd century BCE and decorated with **Jataka tales and scenes from the Buddha's life** (discovered by **Colin Mackenzie**), which lent its name to the distinctive **Amaravati School of Art**. Nearby **Nagarjunakonda**, later enriched by the **Ikshvakus**, is famed for its Buddhist carvings. In the western Deccan, the **Karle Chaitya** — the largest rock-cut Chaitya hall — and **Ajanta Caves 9 and 10** were developed under Satavahana patronage.

In **trade and economy**, the fertile **Krishna–Godavari delta** was a major rice-producing zone using **paddy transplantation**. Commerce flowed along the **Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha** and through ports such as **Kalyani, Sopara, Bharuch and Ganjam**; **coins in lead, copper and bronze** bearing **ship and Chaitya motifs** and **Prakrit legends** attest to buoyant **maritime trade**, including contact with the Roman world.

For **Andhra Pradesh**, the Satavahanas are foundational: identified as the **Andhras** of the Puranas, with Amaravati as a capital and the eponymous art school, they represent the state's first imperial era — hence their high salience for APPSC.
keyPoints: First great Deccan kingdom; capitals Pratishthana (Paithan) and Amaravati.
Amaravati Stupa (AP) → Amaravati School of Art; discovered by Colin Mackenzie.
Nagarjunakonda (AP, later Ikshvaku), Karle Chaitya and Ajanta Caves 9-10 (Maharashtra).
Krishna–Godavari rice economy; trade via Uttarapatha/Dakshinapatha and ports (Kalyani, Sopara, Bharuch, Ganjam).
Lead/copper/bronze coins with ship and Chaitya motifs; maritime (incl. Roman) trade.
AP relevance: 'Andhras' of the Puranas, Amaravati capital and art school — the state's first imperial era.

items.question: Examine the administrative structure and society of the Satavahanas, with special reference to their feudatory system, matronymic tradition and religious policy.
items.modelAnswer:
The Satavahanas evolved a **decentralised administration** that retained several **Mauryan features** but adapted them to Deccan conditions, with a strong emphasis on **regional and military governance and feudal elements**.

**Administrative divisions** ran from the **Janapada** (province) through the **Rashtra** (under a Rashtrika/Maharathi) and **Ahara** (district, under Amatyas/Mahamatras) to the **Vishaya** and finally the **Grama** (village, under a Gramani or the military Gaulmika). A distinctive **feudatory system** graded intermediaries into **Rajas** (the highest, who minted coins in their own names), **Mahabhojas** (Thane–Kolaba) and **Maharathis** (Poona). Military administration used **Katakas** (temporary camps) and **Skandhavaras** (permanent cantonments), while officers like the **Senapati** (commander-cum-governor), **Rajjuka** (revenue), **Bhandagarika** (treasury) and **Paniyagharika** (waterworks) ran the state.

**Society** followed the **varna system**, but thriving trade raised the standing of **merchants and artisans**. The **matronymic tradition** — kings named after their mothers, as in **Gautami-putra** and **Vashishti-putra** — and the prominence of women such as **Nayanika** (regent) and **Gautami Balashri** point to women's elevated status.

In **religion**, the rulers were **Brahmins** who performed **Vedic sacrifices (Ashvamedha, Rajasuya)** yet **patronised Buddhism through land grants** to monks — pioneering the land-grant tradition and embodying a policy of **religious harmony**.
keyPoints: Decentralised, part-Mauryan administration: Janapada > Rashtra > Ahara > Vishaya > Grama.
Feudatory grades: Rajas (minted coins), Mahabhojas, Maharathis; Katakas/Skandhavaras for the military.
Officers: Senapati, Rajjuka, Bhandagarika, Paniyagharika, Karmantika, Avesanika.
Varna society with rising status of merchants and artisans due to trade.
Matronymic tradition (Gautami-putra, Vashishti-putra); influential women (Nayanika, Gautami Balashri).
Brahmin rulers performing Vedic sacrifices while granting land to Buddhist monks — religious harmony.
